item.title: Why The Ubyssey is covering the World Cup
item.description: The Ubyssey sports editor Caleb Peterson applies Jay Rosen’s concept of “awayness” to the newspaper’s decision to cover the 2026 FIFA World Cup. Peterson argues that simply reporting events readers can already watch or find elsewhere does not solve an awayness problem; the publication instead has to add value through beat expertise, analysis and trusted voices.

item.title: Subscribers buy a product. Members join the cause.
item.description: PressThink essay in which Rosen draws a distinction at the heart of journalism's funding debate: subscribers buy a product, members join the cause -- one a transaction, the other a commitment. Drawing on his 2017-2021 Membership Puzzle Project and Talking Points Memo's membership drive, he contrasts subscription models (Wall Street Journal, Financial Times, New York Times's "journalism worth paying for") with membership models such as the Salt Lake Tribune's decision to drop its paywall and treat trustworthy journalism as a right, not a luxury. He argues membership is about solidarity with a cause -- increasingly, chronicling an authoritarian crisis -- and predicts that donating one's knowledge and civic skills will become common practice in journalism.

item.title: For Jay Rosen, American Press Needs to Become More Pro-Democracy
item.description: Interview with Jay Rosen for NYU's Journal of Political Inquiry, conducted by Pau Torres Pages. Rosen argues this is the worst time for American journalism because it is the worst time for American democracy, and presses his case that the American press must become more explicitly pro-democracy -- distilled in his slogan "not the odds but the stakes." He diagnoses the collapse of the Washington Post under Jeff Bezos, proposes a Washington Post Foundation/trust to insulate it from owners, assesses the defunding of public media and the Corporation for Public Broadcasting, and questions Bari Weiss's ideologically driven leadership of CBS. He closes that the powerful will always find ways to be informed; the open question is whether publics, in the plural, will remain so.

item.title: A new fellowship is all about putting the news in news creator
item.description: The Columbia Journalism School is launching the News Creator Fellowship, a year-long program designed to support independent journalists and content creators producing original news outside traditional media. The fellowship will provide a $75,000 stipend, access to university resources, mentorship, workshops, workspace, and collaboration opportunities. The program aims to support individuals from diverse backgrounds producing news content on various platforms and who demonstrate a commitment to public service and pushing the boundaries of news. Applications for the inaugural cohort, starting in September 2026, are open now.

item.title: Public journalism redux: Post-academia, Jay Rosen returns to where he started
item.description: Dan Kennedy profiles Rosen's post-retirement career move as president of News Creator Corps, a new organization that works with content creators to adopt journalism tools without giving up their independence. Kennedy traces Rosen's career from public journalism and Assignment Zero through his media criticism, noting this new role represents a return to Rosen's original mission of involving the public more directly in journalism.
